questions.q: Why does the summary suggest examining your earliest memories of money?
a: They reveal the beliefs blocking good money habits
They show exactly how much you will earn later
They prove that budgeting is too complex to learn
They replace the need for an emergency fund
questions.why: Lesson 1 says childhood experiences with money hold the deeper problems behind overspending, so journaling about them builds awareness.

questions.q: What is the recommended percentage split for a budget?
a: 50 percent fixed costs, 20 percent goals, 30 percent flexible
60 percent fixed costs, 30 percent goals, 10 percent flexible
40 percent fixed costs, 40 percent goals, 20 percent flexible
70 percent fixed costs, 10 percent goals, 20 percent flexible
questions.why: Lesson 2 breaks spending into fixed costs at 50 percent, financial goals at 20 percent and flexible spending at 30 percent.

questions.q: Why does the summary advise keeping your credit cards rather than cutting them up?
a: They build the credit record needed for big purchases
They offer unlimited money with no consequences
They remove the need to track monthly spending
They guarantee approval for a mortgage
questions.why: Lesson 3 says a credit score is a record of managing debt, and lenders rely on it when you want to borrow for a car or house.

questions.q: What rule does the summary recommend for using a credit card?
a: Spend only what you can repay and clear it monthly
Carry a small balance to improve your credit score
Use it only for emergencies and never for daily costs
Pay the minimum each month and invest the rest
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the author promised to charge only what she could pay off and paid the full balance every month, keeping her score above 800.

questions.q: In the New York example, what adjustment does the summary suggest for savings?
a: Start with a smaller amount and raise it with future pay
Skip saving until all fixed costs are eliminated
Borrow the missing amount from a credit card
Move to a cheaper city before saving anything
questions.why: Lesson 2 says when fixed costs reach 60 percent, aiming for 20 percent savings may be unrealistic, so start near $200 and increase it with raises.
